title: Fitting a fence post with a concrete spur
subtitle: Bolt a concrete repair spur to a rotted fence post base and set it in concrete to restore the post without replacing the full length
excerpt: How to repair a fence post that has rotted at ground level using a concrete spur. Covers excavating around the post base, positioning and levelling the spur, bolting it to the post, and concreting it in.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade fencing practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pre-cast concrete post repair spur, typically 600 to 750 mm long and 100 x 100 mm section, with pre-drilled holes for through-bolts. It is sunk into the ground beside the damaged timber post and bolted to the sound upper section, giving a new concrete foundation without replacing the full post.

content.text: When a fence post rots at ground level but the upper section is still sound, a
gives a new foundation without removing the whole post. The spur bolts to the existing timber and is concreted in beside it. BEGINNER: basic digging and bolting; no special skills needed.

Dig out the soil alongside the post on the side where the spur will go, to a depth of at least 600 mm and wide enough to lower the spur into the hole beside the post. If the old post base is in a concrete socket, break out enough of the old concrete to create room for the spur. Remove all loose soil and debris from the hole.
Cut away the rotten section of post

Saw through the rotten section of the timber post at the point where the wood is firm. Remove the rotted lower stub. The upper section of the post should be treated with a wood preservative applied to the freshly cut end grain before the spur is bolted on.
Position the spur and drill through bolts

Lower the spur into the hole alongside the cut post end. Align the pre-drilled bolt holes in the spur with the post face, and mark through the holes onto the timber. Drill through the timber with the correct diameter bit. Push coach bolts through the spur holes and through the drilled holes in the post timber. Fit washers and nuts and tighten firmly.
Check for plumb and concrete in

Check the post is plumb in both directions with the spirit level. Prop the post upright with temporary braces if needed. Mix a stiff batch of post-fixing concrete and pour into the hole around the spur. Compact with a timber rod to remove air pockets. Mound the concrete slightly above ground level around the spur and slope it away from the post to shed water. Leave to cure for at least two days before removing any bracing.

attrs.symptom: Post is still not rigid after the concrete has set
attrs.cause: The spur was not buried deep enough, or the concrete did not fill all the voids around the spur.
attrs.fix: Excavate around the spur, break out the loose concrete, and relay with a deeper spur if possible. Pack fresh concrete firmly around the full spur length.

attrs.symptom: Bolts are hard to tighten and the spur sits slightly away from the post face
attrs.cause: The bolt holes in the spur and the timber are slightly misaligned.
attrs.fix: Elongate one of the holes in the timber with a round file to allow the bolt to pull through. Use large penny washers to bridge any remaining gap.
